opus-5.5.text:
Well, I come at this as a physicist, and I think the history of physics gives us a lot of reason for optimism here. If you think about something like a gas in a room, you've got on the order of 10^23 molecules bouncing around, and in principle that's hopelessly complicated. You could never track every particle. But it turns out you don't need to. Statistical mechanics and thermodynamics let you describe that system with a handful of quantities like temperature, pressure, and volume, and those descriptions are incredibly accurate. The complexity at the microscopic level washes out, and simple, effective laws emerge at the macroscopic level.

I think neural networks are very similar in spirit. You've got billions or trillions of parameters, and you might think that means they're fundamentally inscrutable black boxes. But the large number of components is actually what helps us. When you have many parts, there's often a kind of averaging that happens, and you can find principles that govern the behavior of the whole system without understanding every individual weight. That's a big part of what I tried to do in the work on the principles of deep learning theory: take ideas from physics, like expansions around a simple limit, the infinite-width limit, and then study the corrections, and show that you can actually derive meaningful, quantitative predictions about how these networks behave and learn.

And there's empirical evidence that this kind of regularity exists. Scaling laws are a great example. People found that as you increase model size, data, and compute, the loss improves in a remarkably smooth and predictable way. That's exactly the kind of thing a physicist gets excited about, because smooth, simple laws emerging from a messy system usually signal that there's some underlying theory waiting to be discovered.

So I'd say the reasons are: one, we've seen this movie before in physics, where enormous complexity gives way to simple effective descriptions; two, we have the advantage that, unlike nature, we built these systems, so we can probe them, run controlled experiments, and inspect every component; and three, the empirical regularities we already observe strongly suggest there's real structure there to understand. It's not going to be easy, but I don't think it's hopeless at all. I think it's one of the most exciting scientific problems of our time.

r001.rationale: It draws a direct analogy to physics, where complex systems yield simple effective laws, and says that history gives reason for optimism about understanding AI systems.

r002.rationale: It says that with many components, averaging can occur, allowing principles of the whole system to be understood without tracking every individual weight.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So my background is in theoretical physics, and I think the honest answer is that I come at this with a kind of physicist's optimism. If you look at the history of physics, over and over we've encountered systems that seemed hopelessly complicated, with an enormous number of interacting parts, and found that they're actually governed by relatively simple principles once you find the right variables to describe them. Thermodynamics is the classic example. You have something like ten to the twenty-three molecules bouncing around in a box, and nobody can track each one, but it turns out you don't need to. Temperature, pressure, entropy, a handful of macroscopic quantities capture almost everything you care about. Statistical mechanics then explains why that works.

Neural networks have a very similar flavor to me. They have billions of parameters, they're trained on messy data with stochastic optimization, and it's tempting to say this is just an engineering artifact, an inscrutable pile of numbers, and the best we can do is run experiments. But the fact that these systems are large is actually what makes them tractable, not what makes them hopeless. When you have a huge number of components, you get collective behavior that's often simpler than the behavior of any individual component. Scaling laws are a hint of exactly that. The fact that loss follows these clean power laws across orders of magnitude in compute and data is not what you'd expect from a system with no underlying regularity. That's the kind of empirical signature that, in physics, tells you there's a theory waiting to be found.

The other thing I'd say is that we have an unusual advantage here compared to, say, neuroscience. We built these things. We know the architecture exactly, we know the training procedure, we can read out every weight and every activation, and we can run the same experiment a thousand times with different random seeds. In almost every other area of science you're fighting for access to the system. Here the object of study is completely open to us. So the question isn't really whether understanding is possible in principle. It's whether we're asking the right questions and developing the right mathematical tools, and I think the early work on things like infinite-width limits, feature learning, and effective theories of deep networks suggests we're starting to.

r001.rationale: It points to physics’ success in finding simple principles for systems with many interacting parts and uses that as an analogy for why neural networks may be scientifically understandable.

r002.rationale: It says large systems can show simpler collective behavior and mentions macroscopic quantities and statistical mechanics, but does not clearly identify statistical averaging as the mechanism producing that simplicity.

astra-6.text:
Well, complexity by itself doesn’t mean something is beyond scientific understanding. In physics, we study systems with enormous numbers of interacting components, and we can often find principles that explain their collective behavior without tracking every component individually.

I think there’s a similar opportunity with AI. A neural network has a huge number of parameters, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you need an equally huge number of ideas to understand what it does. You can make controlled experiments, propose simplified models, and test whether those models predict what happens when you change the network or its training.

That’s not a guarantee that we’ll get a complete theory. But we don’t need a complete theory to make progress. We need explanations that make useful, testable predictions—and then we can build from there.

r001.rationale: The response points to physics explaining systems with many interacting components, then draws a similar opportunity for understanding AI systems.

r002.rationale: It mentions collective behavior in large systems but does not identify statistical averaging as the mechanism that can produce simplicity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that complexity doesn’t necessarily prevent understanding. A gas contains an enormous number of molecules, and we can’t track every one of them, but we can still develop precise laws for things like temperature and pressure. The challenge is finding the right level of description.

With AI, we know the rules used to train the system, and we can run controlled experiments. We can change the architecture, the data, or the amount of training and ask which behaviors change predictably. That gives us a way to test theories.

That doesn’t mean we’ll be able to predict every word a model produces. But we can hope to understand why certain capabilities emerge, when a model will generalize, and where our explanations break down. Those are scientific questions, even when the underlying system is very complicated.

r001.rationale: The response uses our ability to describe a gas with precise laws despite its many molecules as a reason to expect scientific understanding of complex AI systems.

r002.rationale: It mentions describing temperature and pressure without tracking every molecule, but does not identify statistical averaging as the mechanism producing that simplicity.
